description: We’re a team interested in space, coding, and AI. We want to build something useful and learn together. We’re looking for teammates who like coding, design, working with data, or sharing ideas.
summary:
Crimson Horizon is an interactive web app for planning astronaut walks on real Martian terrain. Users choose a start, an end and up to 8 stops in Jezero or Gusev crater and set how steep a slope the crew may climb. The app then compares two routes: the shortest path and a gentler path that avoids steep and rough ground. For each it shows distance, climb, steepest point and walking time, on a 2D map, in 3D and on a globe of Mars.

This addresses the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge by turning NASA orbital elevation maps, rover tracks and mission records into a practical survival tool. At Hawksbill Gap, routes built from Perseverance’s real drives are checked for hidden steep steps, timed for a spacesuit walk and linked to real rock sample sites.
details:
What you can do

Plan your own walk. Place a start, an end and up to 8 stops in Jezero or Gusev crater. Use a slider to set how steep a slope the crew may climb.

Compare two options. See the shortest route and a gentler one that avoids steep and rough ground, each with its distance, total climb, steepest point and walking time.

See the ground in 3D. Fly over the real terrain with your route drawn on it, and follow the elevation profile to see where the climbs are.

Explore a real mission scenario. At Hawksbill Gap, compare two routes built from Perseverance’s real drives. You get caution zones, a time budget for the spacesuit walk and science stops at places where the rover collected rock samples.

Check the conditions. View local weather recorded by Perseverance and the radiation background measured on the Martian surface.

Travel the planet. Spin a 3D globe of Mars and visit places where Perseverance and Spirit worked, each with a short story and its source.

Take the plan with you. Export routes and caution zones as a map file.

The data

Everything comes from real, cited NASA and USGS sources: high-resolution orbital elevation maps, rover tracks, rock sample records and weather measurements. Nothing is invented. Where the data is uncertain, for example where two elevation maps disagree, the app says so instead of calling a route “safe”.

GitHub Link

Who it is for

Students and teachers who want to learn how missions read Mars from orbit.

Space enthusiasts who want to explore real rover sites.

Mission concept teams who need a quick, transparent first look at a crewed walk before detailed engineering work.
